The question of whether the Temple of Solomon was real is a matter of ongoing scholarly debate with conflicting research outcomes. According to Britannica, "nearly all evidence for Solomon's life and reign comes from the Bible," and "material evidence for Solomon's reign, as for that of his father, is scant" [d5]. Similarly, the Biblical Archaeology Society reports that "for centuries, scholars have searched in vain for any remnant of Solomon's Temple," partly because excavation on Jerusalem's Temple Mount is impossible [d6]. However, d6 also notes that the Iron Age 'Ain Dara temple in northern Syria shares "more than 30 architectural and decorative elements" with the biblical description, providing indirect architectural support for the Temple's plausibility [d6]. On the other side, ancient Muslim texts cited by the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs — including writings by al-Tabari and al-Idrisi — explicitly confirm the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem and describe Solomon's construction on the Temple Mount, standing "against claims that invert the truth, according to which 'the legend of the bogus Temple is the greatest crime of historical forgery'" [d7]. A further fringe scholarly theory, proposed by Ahmed Osman, suggests that no archaeological discovery speaks of King David or Solomon "directly or indirectly," and that the Temple of Solomon may correspond to the Mortuary Temple of Luxor in Egypt [d2]. In sum, while the biblical and some ancient textual traditions affirm the Temple's existence [d3, d7], mainstream archaeology has yet to produce direct physical evidence, leaving the question unresolved among researchers [d5, d6].
